stemMd: In the coding sequence of a gene, a single nucleotide is deleted a few bases after the start codon. No other change occurs. What is the most likely effect on the protein encoded by the gene?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Only one amino acid is changed; the rest of the protein is normal

options.label: B
options.textMd: One amino acid is missing; the rest of the protein is normal

options.label: C
options.textMd: There is no change, because the genetic code is redundant

options.label: D
options.textMd: The reading frame shifts, changing most amino acids after the deletion

options.label: E
options.textMd: An extra amino acid is inserted at the point of the deletion

explanationMd:
The code is read in **triplets** (codons) from the start codon onward, with no punctuation between them. Removing one nucleotide shifts every later grouping by one position.

For example, the message `AUG GCA UUC GAA ...` with the first `G` of `GCA` deleted becomes `AUG CAU UCG AA...`: every codon after the deletion is new. The amino-acid sequence is altered from that point on, and a stop codon often appears early, cutting the protein short. This is a **frameshift mutation**, and near the start of the gene it usually destroys the protein's function.

**Check:** to remove exactly one amino acid and leave the frame intact, three adjacent nucleotides (a whole codon) would have to be deleted. One nucleotide is not a multiple of three, so the frame must shift.

distractorRationale.a: Changing a single amino acid is the typical effect of a substitution (a missense mutation), where the number of nucleotides stays the same and the frame is kept.
distractorRationale.b: Losing exactly one amino acid requires the deletion of three nucleotides, a whole codon. Deleting one nucleotide shifts the frame instead.
distractorRationale.c: Redundancy can hide a substitution in the third base of a codon (a silent mutation). It cannot hide a deletion, which changes how every following codon is grouped.
distractorRationale.e: An insertion of nucleotides, not a deletion, would be needed to add material; and even an inserted single nucleotide would shift the frame rather than add one amino acid.

accessibilityText: A short text question with no figure. In the coding sequence of a gene, one nucleotide is deleted a few bases after the start codon. The question asks the most likely effect on the encoded protein. The choices are: only one amino acid changes and the rest is normal; one amino acid is missing and the rest is normal; no change, because the genetic code is redundant; the reading frame shifts, changing most amino acids after the deletion; an extra amino acid is inserted at the deletion point. The explanation shows an example message read in groups of three letters.

provenance.notes: Original item. Tests the effect of a single-nucleotide deletion as a frameshift mutation, contrasted with substitutions and codon deletions.
